ideologies.desc: The charter city idea, from Paul Romer, holds that new cities with their own clear rules can speed growth in poor regions. A trusted outside partner may help run the city. Holders favour exit and rule of law.

ideologies.name: panarchy
ideologies.desc: Panarchy holds that people should choose freely among competing governments that serve members, not territory. Each person joins the legal system that suits that person, and may leave it at will.

ideologies.name: futarchy
ideologies.desc: Futarchy is a system proposed by Robin Hanson. Voters set the goals of government, and prediction markets decide which policies best reach those goals. Holders trust markets to find facts better than votes or officials.

ideologies.name: liquid democracy
ideologies.desc: Liquid democracy lets each citizen vote on a law directly or pass that vote to a trusted delegate. A citizen can take the vote back at any time. Holders see it as a blend of direct and representative rule.

ideologies.name: demarchy
ideologies.desc: Demarchy is rule by citizens chosen by lot. Many small bodies of random citizens handle each public function, in place of elected parties. Holders say this lowers the pull of money and party.

ideologies.name: world federalism
ideologies.desc: World federalism holds that nations should join in a federal world government with power over war, trade and the global commons. Holders favour a world parliament, a world court and a ban on national armies.

ideologies.name: posadism
ideologies.desc: Posadism is a Trotskyist current led by J. Posadas. It holds that nuclear war would lead to socialism and that advanced extraterrestrial societies are socialist. Posadists favour revolution and a planned economy.

ideologies.name: left accelerationism
ideologies.desc: Left accelerationism holds that capitalism should be pushed past its limits by its own technology, and that the tools it builds should serve common ends. Holders favour automation, a post-work society and planning.

ideologies.name: right accelerationism
ideologies.desc: Right accelerationism, linked to Nick Land, holds that capitalism and technology should speed up and undo social bonds and old institutions. Many holders also favour hierarchy and view democracy as slow or weak.

ideologies.name: antinatalism
ideologies.desc: Antinatalism holds that coming into existence is a harm, so people should not have children. Most holders rest this on the weight of suffering and consent. Many favour voluntary choice and ban no one.

ideologies.name: animal liberation
ideologies.desc: Animal liberation holds that the interests of animals count equally with like human interests, so people should end farming and testing that cause pain. Holders use law, campaigns and consumer choice.

ideologies.name: esperantism
ideologies.desc: Esperantism is the political strand of the Esperanto movement. It holds that a neutral shared second language helps peace and equality between nations. Holders favour equal language rights and international understanding.

ideologies.name: neocameralism
ideologies.desc: Neocameralism is a proposal of Curtis Yarvin. It holds that a state should run as a joint-stock company with a chief executive and owners who gain from good management. It rejects democracy and mass politics.

ideologies.name: AI pause
ideologies.desc: The AI pause position holds that advanced artificial intelligence may pose grave risk. States should limit or halt training of the strongest systems until they are safe. Holders favour treaties and audits.

ideologies.name: free software movement
ideologies.desc: The free software movement holds that users should be free to run, study, share and change software. Holders favour copyleft licences and open standards, and they oppose locks that bar users from their own devices.

ideologies.name: space settlement
ideologies.desc: This position, tied to Cosmism and Gerard O'Neill, holds that humanity should spread into space for survival and growth. Holders support large public and private space programs, off-world cities and use of space resources.

ideologies.name: Kemalism
ideologies.desc: Kemalism is the founding doctrine of the Turkish republic, set out by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. Its six principles are republicanism, nationalism, populism, statism, secularism and reformism. It places the nation above faith in public life.

ideologies.name: Peronism
ideologies.desc: Peronism is the movement of Juan Peron in Argentina. It rests on social justice, economic independence and political sovereignty, and it joins organised labour with a strong leader. Peronism has left and right wings.

ideologies.name: Nasserism
ideologies.desc: Nasserism is the doctrine of Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt. It combines Arab nationalism, state-led development, land reform and non-alignment in world affairs. It rests on one national party and a strong president.

ideologies.name: Ba'athism
ideologies.desc: Ba'athism is an Arab nationalist doctrine of unity, freedom and socialism. It seeks one Arab nation, a secular state and public control of the economy. Ba'athist parties ruled Syria and Iraq as one-party states, and their governments killed tens of thousands in the Anfal campaign and at Hama in 1982.

ideologies.name: Juche
ideologies.desc: Juche is the state ideology of North Korea, set out by Kim Il Sung. It holds that the people master their own fate, and it stresses self-reliance under one party and a supreme leader. The state runs political prison camps, and a famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands.

ideologies.name: Titoism
ideologies.desc: Titoism is the doctrine of Josip Broz Tito in Yugoslavia. It holds to a communist single-party state with worker self-management, a market element and non-alignment in the Cold War. It kept ethnic nations in one federation.

ideologies.name: Castroism
ideologies.desc: Castroism is the doctrine of Fidel Castro in Cuba. It holds to a one-party socialist state, a planned economy, free public health and schooling, and defiance of the United States. After 1959 its government executed hundreds of opponents and jailed thousands for political reasons.

ideologies.name: Chavismo
ideologies.desc: Chavismo, or Bolivarianism, is the movement of Hugo Chavez in Venezuela. It joins 21st century socialism, social programs funded by oil, regional unity and anti-imperial politics with rule by a strong president and communal councils.

ideologies.name: Sankarism
ideologies.desc: Sankarism is the doctrine of Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso. It joins anti-imperial politics, self-reliance, land reform, women's rights and a clean public service. It was a revolutionary program led by a military government.

ideologies.name: Zapatismo
ideologies.desc: Zapatismo is the doctrine of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation in Chiapas. It seeks indigenous autonomy, land, dignity and rule by communities that "lead by obeying". It began with an armed rising in 1994 and turned to civil self-government.

ideologies.name: Ujamaa
ideologies.desc: Ujamaa is the African socialism of Julius Nyerere in Tanzania. It rests on family-like cooperation, self-reliance and collective village farming. It ran under one party with local participation.

ideologies.name: Gandhism
ideologies.desc: Gandhism is the thought of Mohandas Gandhi. It rests on nonviolent resistance, truth, village self-rule, simple living and religious tolerance. It seeks a decentralised India of self-reliant communities.

ideologies.name: Three Principles of the People
ideologies.desc: The Three Principles of Sun Yat-sen are nationalism, democracy and the livelihood of the people. They seek national independence, constitutional rule in stages and land equalisation with public ownership of key industry.

ideologies.name: Gaullism
ideologies.desc: Gaullism is the doctrine of Charles de Gaulle. It stresses a strong president above party, national independence in defence and foreign policy, social partnership and the grandeur of France.

ideologies.name: Thatcherism
ideologies.desc: Thatcherism is the program of Margaret Thatcher in Britain. It favours free markets, privatisation, lower union power, tight money, low tax and a strong defence. It places the individual and the household before the state.

ideologies.name: Reaganism
ideologies.desc: Reaganism is the program of Ronald Reagan in the United States. It favours tax cuts, less regulation, a strong military, firm opposition to the Soviet Union and traditional values. It trusts markets and local rule over federal power.

ideologies.name: Pan-Africanism
ideologies.desc: Pan-Africanism holds that people of African descent share a common history and fate, and should unite. Its aims range from cultural solidarity to a political union of African states, with an end to colonial rule and racism.

ideologies.name: pan-Arabism
ideologies.desc: Pan-Arabism holds that Arabs form one nation, and that Arab states should unite in politics and economy. It stresses a shared language, history and culture, and many of its parties stress independence from foreign powers.

ideologies.name: pan-Slavism
ideologies.desc: Pan-Slavism, from the 19th century, holds that Slavic peoples share common roots and should cooperate or unite. Its forms range from cultural revival to political union under a leading power, and some forms seek protection of Orthodox peoples.

ideologies.name: Zionism
ideologies.desc: Zionism is the national movement of the Jewish people for a state in their ancestral land. Its political mainstream seeks a Jewish and democratic state with a Jewish majority, shared with minorities. The founding of Israel in 1948 caused the flight or expulsion of about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs.

ideologies.name: Kirchnerism
ideologies.desc: Kirchnerism is the current of Nestor and Cristina Kirchner in Argentina, within Peronism. It favours state-led growth, social spending, human rights trials, trade protection and regional cooperation, with a strong role for the president.

ideologies.name: Dengism
ideologies.desc: Dengism is the program of Deng Xiaoping in China. It holds that socialism needs growth, so it allows markets and foreign trade under Communist Party rule, and it puts stability first. Deng approved the military suppression of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests.

ideologies.name: Putinism
ideologies.desc: Putinism is the style of rule built by Vladimir Putin in Russia. It stresses a strong state and president, national sovereignty, traditional values, a state role in key industry and a great-power foreign policy. Under Putin, Russia fought wars in Chechnya and Georgia and in 2022 began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

ideologies.name: Khomeinism
ideologies.desc: Khomeinism is the doctrine of Ruhollah Khomeini. It holds that a leading jurist should guard an Islamic republic under Islamic law, called velayat-e faqih, free of foreign influence. The state it founded in 1979 executed thousands of political prisoners, many of them in 1988.

ideologies.name: Jacksonian democracy
ideologies.desc: Jacksonian democracy is the movement of Andrew Jackson in the 19th century United States. It sought wider white male suffrage, rule by common citizens, no national bank and the defence of slavery. Its Indian removal policy forced about 60,000 Native Americans from their lands, and thousands died.

ideologies.name: Jeffersonian democracy
ideologies.desc: Jeffersonian democracy holds that a republic of independent farmers and small property owners is the base of liberty. It favours limited national government, state rights, free speech and religious freedom, with little public debt.

ideologies.name: democratic confederalism
ideologies.desc: Democratic confederalism is the model of the Kurdish movement and the self-administration in Rojava, from the thought of Abdullah Ocalan. It seeks stateless self-rule by councils, women's equality, ecology and ethnic coexistence.

ideologies.name: Nehruvian socialism
ideologies.desc: Nehruvian socialism is the program of Jawaharlal Nehru in India. It joins parliamentary democracy and secularism with a mixed economy, five-year plans, public heavy industry, science and non-alignment.

ideologies.name: Lee Kuan Yew's pragmatism
ideologies.desc: This doctrine guided Singapore under Lee Kuan Yew. It stresses order, clean and expert government, open trade, multiracial policy, thrift and one dominant party. It holds that social needs come before individual claims.

ideologies.name: Orbanism
ideologies.desc: Orbanism is the program of Viktor Orban in Hungary. It stresses national sovereignty, Christian and family values, state control of key sectors and sceptical views of migration and of the European Union. Its supporters call it illiberal democracy.

ideologies.name: Erdoganism
ideologies.desc: Erdoganism is the program of Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey. It joins conservative and religious values, state-backed construction and growth, a strong presidency and an assertive foreign policy. Critics point to limits on press and courts.

ideologies.name: Sandinismo
ideologies.desc: Sandinismo is the thought of the Sandinista movement in Nicaragua, named for Augusto Sandino. It seeks national independence, land reform, literacy, a mixed economy and popular participation. It rose through a revolution against the Somoza family.

ideologies.name: Trumpism
ideologies.desc: Trumpism is the politics of Donald Trump in the United States. It stresses national interest first, tariffs, lower migration, scepticism of alliances and trade deals, and a strong executive. It draws on populist and conservative views.

ideologies.name: Hindutva
ideologies.desc: Hindutva is a Hindu nationalist ideology set out by V. D. Savarkar. It holds that India is a nation rooted in Hindu culture and civilisation, and it seeks a unified national culture and a strong state. Its movement led the campaign that ended in the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid, and communal riots followed.

ideologies.name: Lulismo
ideologies.desc: Lulismo is the politics of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil. It joins market growth with cash transfers, a higher minimum wage, access to education and bargaining between classes. It works by coalition and compromise.

ideologies.name: Black Consciousness
ideologies.desc: Black Consciousness is the movement of Steve Biko in South Africa. It holds that Black people should claim pride, self-reliance and psychological freedom, and organise themselves, as the base of liberation from white minority rule.

ideologies.name: Yoshida doctrine
ideologies.desc: The Yoshida doctrine guided Japan after 1945. It relies on the United States for defence, keeps military spending low and puts national effort into economic recovery and trade. It rests on the postwar peace constitution.

ideologies.name: conservatism
ideologies.desc: Conservatism values inherited institutions, customs and gradual change. It holds that social order grows over time and that sudden redesign risks harm. It backs private property, a limited but firm state and the rule of law.

ideologies.name: one-nation conservatism
ideologies.desc: One-nation conservatism, also called progressive conservatism, holds that the rich owe duties to the poor and that society is one body. It backs a mixed economy, public services and a cohesive national life. It prefers gradual reform to class conflict.

ideologies.name: fiscal conservatism
ideologies.desc: Fiscal conservatism calls for low taxes, restrained public spending and balanced budgets. It sees public debt as a burden on later generations. It prefers markets to state programmes.

ideologies.name: social conservatism
ideologies.desc: Social conservatism defends traditional family structure, religious morals and established social norms. It backs laws that support marriage and limit practices it holds to harm the moral order. It is often wary of rapid cultural change.

ideologies.name: national conservatism
ideologies.desc: National conservatism joins conservative values with a strong view of the nation and its borders. It backs lower migration, family policy, tariffs on key goods and national sovereignty. It accepts a more active state than classical conservatism.

ideologies.name: paleoconservatism
ideologies.desc: Paleoconservatism stresses tradition, local community, religion and national sovereignty. It opposes foreign wars, large federal power, mass migration and free trade deals. It distrusts both the managerial state and corporate globalism.

ideologies.name: neoconservatism
ideologies.desc: Neoconservatism backs an active foreign policy that promotes liberal democracy and American power abroad. It holds market economies and a strong military to be sound. At home it defends traditional institutions and criticizes cultural liberalism.

ideologies.name: traditionalist conservatism
ideologies.desc: Traditionalist conservatism, in the line of Burke and Russell Kirk, treats moral order as real and inherited. It values community, religion, local custom and prudence. It distrusts ideology and rapid reform.

ideologies.name: burkean conservatism
ideologies.desc: Burkean conservatism holds that society is a partnership across generations. It trusts inherited institutions and slow reform over abstract plans. It values prescription, prudence and the small groups between person and state.

ideologies.name: green conservatism
ideologies.desc: Green conservatism treats nature as an inheritance to keep and pass on. It backs market tools, local stewardship and gradual policy to protect land, air and water. It links conservation to tradition and property.

ideologies.name: compassionate conservatism
ideologies.desc: Compassionate conservatism holds that conservative principles serve the poor best through faith groups, charities and local programmes. It backs market economics with targeted public help. It stresses personal responsibility and moral renewal.

ideologies.name: fusionism
ideologies.desc: Fusionism joins free-market economics, traditional moral order and strong anti-communism in one movement. It holds that liberty needs virtue and virtue needs liberty. It shaped the American postwar right.

ideologies.name: christian right
ideologies.desc: The Christian right is a political movement of conservative Christians who seek to shape law by biblical morals. It opposes abortion and same-sex marriage and backs religious liberty and school prayer. It works through elections and party politics.

ideologies.name: religious conservatism
ideologies.desc: Religious conservatism holds that faith gives the basis of moral order and should shape public life. It backs traditional family roles, religious education and law that reflects religious ethics. It exists in many faiths.

ideologies.name: integralism
ideologies.desc: Integralism holds that political power should serve the spiritual good, and that the state should be ordered under the authority of the Church. It rejects the separation of church and state. Catholic integralism cites papal teaching on social order.

ideologies.name: theocracy
ideologies.desc: Theocracy is rule by religious authority, where divine law is the source of the legal order. Clergy or religious law hold final power over the state. Forms differ by faith and country.

ideologies.name: constitutional monarchism
ideologies.desc: Constitutional monarchism supports a monarch as head of state under a constitution, with elected government doing the daily work. It holds that the crown gives continuity and a symbol above party. It backs the rule of law.

ideologies.name: absolute monarchism
ideologies.desc: Absolute monarchism holds that the monarch has full sovereign power, not bound by a legislature or constitution. It rests the crown on tradition, divine right or inherited duty. Ministers serve the monarch.

ideologies.name: legitimism
ideologies.desc: Legitimism backs the claim of the senior hereditary line to a throne, as the legal dynasty displaced by revolution or usurpation. In French history it opposed the Orleans and Bonaparte lines. It joins dynastic right with throne and altar.

ideologies.name: reactionism
ideologies.desc: Reactionism seeks a return to an earlier social order that it holds to be better, and it opposes modern reforms. It values hierarchy, tradition and settled authority over progress. It differs from conservatism by seeking restoration, not preservation.

ideologies.name: neoreaction
ideologies.desc: Neoreaction, or the dark enlightenment, rejects egalitarian democracy and progressive ideas. It holds that sovereign power should be unified and run like a firm or a monarchy. It mixes reactionary thought with technology and market ideas.

ideologies.name: orleanism
ideologies.desc: Orleanism backs a constitutional monarchy of the House of Orleans in France, a middle way between absolute monarchy and republic. It values a limited franchise, liberal institutions and order. It favours property owners and gradual reform.

ideologies.name: ultramontanism
ideologies.desc: Ultramontanism stresses the authority of the pope over national churches and over civil rulers in matters of faith and morals. It opposed the liberal state and church control by governments. It was strongest in the nineteenth century.

ideologies.name: carlism
ideologies.desc: Carlism is a Spanish traditionalist movement that backed the Carlist line to the throne. Its motto is God, fatherland, fueros, king. It defends the Catholic faith, regional charters and a monarchy limited by tradition.

ideologies.name: christian reconstructionism
ideologies.desc: Christian reconstructionism holds that civil law should follow biblical law and that Christians should bring all areas of life under it. It favours a decentralized order of families, churches and local courts. It rejects state control of schools.

ideologies.name: traditionalist catholicism
ideologies.desc: Traditionalist Catholicism keeps the pre-Vatican II liturgy and doctrine and rejects many reforms that followed. In politics it backs the social kingship of Christ, family order and distrust of liberal modernity. Views on the state vary.

ideologies.name: christian nationalism
ideologies.desc: Christian nationalism holds that a nation should be defined by Christian faith and that law should reflect it. It joins national pride with public religion. Supporters differ on whether it needs an established church.

ideologies.name: minarchism
ideologies.desc: Minarchism holds that the state should be limited to the defence of person and property: police, courts and armed forces. Any wider role breaks individual rights. It differs from anarcho-capitalism by keeping a state.

ideologies.name: anarcho-capitalism
ideologies.desc: Anarcho-capitalism seeks to replace the state with private property, voluntary contract and competing private firms for law and defence. It holds that taxation is theft. It rests on self-ownership and the non-aggression principle.

ideologies.name: paleolibertarianism
ideologies.desc: Paleolibertarianism joins libertarian economics with cultural conservatism, local community and property rights. It opposes the welfare state and centralized power. It holds that a free society needs strong private institutions such as family and church.

ideologies.name: objectivism
ideologies.desc: Objectivism is the philosophy of Ayn Rand. It holds reason as the only source of knowledge, rational self-interest as the basis of ethics and laissez-faire capitalism as the just system. It backs a minimal state that protects rights.

ideologies.name: right-libertarianism
ideologies.desc: Right-libertarianism holds that people own themselves and may acquire and trade property without state limits. It backs free markets and strong property rights, and rejects redistribution. Views on the size of the state vary.

ideologies.name: hoppeanism
ideologies.desc: Hoppeanism follows Hans-Hermann Hoppe in joining a private law society with argumentation ethics. It backs strict covenant communities that may exclude members who reject their norms. It holds democracy to be inferior to monarchy.

ideologies.name: right-wing populism
ideologies.desc: Right-wing populism, also called national populism, sets the ordinary people against an established class it holds to be out of touch. It joins nationalism, cultural conservatism and distrust of institutions. It puts native citizens first on migration, trade and sovereignty.

ideologies.name: ethnonationalism
ideologies.desc: Ethnonationalism defines the nation by shared ethnic descent, language and culture. It holds that the state should serve one ethnic nation and that membership follows ancestry. It limits migration and citizenship.

ideologies.name: civic nationalism
ideologies.desc: Civic nationalism defines the nation by shared citizenship, law and political values, not by ancestry. Anyone may join who accepts the civic creed. It ties national pride to liberty and equal rights.

ideologies.name: economic nationalism
ideologies.desc: Economic nationalism uses tariffs, subsidies and state guidance to build national industry and protect jobs. It holds the economy to be a tool of national strength. It prefers domestic control of key sectors.

ideologies.name: sovereigntism
ideologies.desc: Sovereigntism holds that a nation should keep final authority over its own law, borders and policy, and should resist transfers of power to international bodies. It is found on the right and the left. On the right it is often tied to nationalism.

ideologies.name: welfare chauvinism
ideologies.desc: Welfare chauvinism backs a generous welfare state but limits its benefits to native citizens or long-term residents. It joins social spending with restriction of migration. It is common among nationalist parties in Europe.

ideologies.name: tea party conservatism
ideologies.desc: Tea Party conservatism is an American movement for lower taxes, smaller federal government, lower debt and strict readings of the constitution. It opposes bailouts and new federal programmes. It grew from 2009.

ideologies.name: nativism
ideologies.desc: Nativism favours the interests of established inhabitants over those of immigrants. It backs low migration, strict naturalisation and the defence of the existing national culture. Forms differ by country and period.

ideologies.name: fascism
ideologies.desc: Fascism puts the nation or race above the individual and calls for a single party, a strong leader and a state that directs society. It rejects liberalism, socialism and parliamentary democracy and values national rebirth through struggle. Fascist regimes in Italy and elsewhere ran one-party dictatorships, waged wars of conquest and persecuted political opponents and minorities.

ideologies.name: national socialism
ideologies.desc: National socialism, or Nazism, was the ideology of the German Nazi Party. It joined racial nationalism, antisemitism, one-party dictatorship and a state-directed economy under the leader principle. The Nazi regime started the Second World War and carried out the Holocaust, which killed about six million Jews, and other mass murder.

ideologies.name: falangism
ideologies.desc: Falangism is the Spanish fascist-inspired movement of the Falange. It stresses Spanish national unity, empire, Catholic tradition and a corporatist state with a single party. After 1937 the Falange served the Franco regime, which held power until 1975.

ideologies.name: clerical fascism
ideologies.desc: Clerical fascism joins fascist politics with religious doctrine and church institutions. It treats the nation as a religious community and backs a one-party state with clergy in public roles. Examples include Austria under Dollfuss and Slovakia under Tiso, whose state deported about 58,000 Jews to Nazi camps in 1942.

ideologies.name: francoism
ideologies.desc: Francoism was the ideology of the Spanish regime of Francisco Franco from 1939 to 1975. It combined authoritarian rule, national Catholicism, anti-communism, Spanish unity and a corporatist economy. The regime banned parties and unions, censored the press and executed tens of thousands of opponents after the civil war.

ideologies.name: integral nationalism
ideologies.desc: Integral nationalism, from Charles Maurras and Action Francaise, holds that the nation is an organic whole that comes before the individual. It values order, hierarchy, tradition and the Catholic heritage of France. It rejects liberal democracy and often backs monarchy.

ideologies.name: southern agrarianism
ideologies.desc: Southern agrarianism, from the 1930 manifesto I Will Take My Stand, defends a rural, craft and family way of life against industrial capitalism. It values tradition, local community and the land. It criticises machine-driven progress.

ideologies.name: corporatism
ideologies.desc: Corporatism organizes society into functional bodies such as industries, trades and professions. These bodies bargain under state supervision in place of class conflict. It has been used by Catholic, fascist and democratic regimes.

ideologies.name: national syndicalism
ideologies.desc: National syndicalism joins syndicalist organisation of workers with nationalism and rejects liberal democracy and parliament. It sees the nation as a union of producers under state direction. It influenced Spanish and Italian fascism.

ideologies.name: strasserism
ideologies.desc: Strasserism is a left-leaning wing of early German National Socialism, named for Gregor and Otto Strasser. It stressed nationalism, anticapitalism, workers rights and nationalization alongside racial doctrine. The Nazi leadership purged it in 1934.

ideologies.name: third position
ideologies.desc: The third position is a far-right current that claims to stand against both capitalism and communism. It joins nationalism, economic localism, anticapitalism and hierarchy. It cites Strasserism, Italian fascism and distributism.

ideologies.name: ultranationalism
ideologies.desc: Ultranationalism holds national interest above all other aims and often calls for national dominance, purity or expansion. It supports a strong military and takes a hard line on minorities and rivals. It appears in many countries and periods.

ideologies.name: authoritarian conservatism
ideologies.desc: Authoritarian conservatism backs strong, centralized rule to keep order and preserve traditional institutions. It limits political opposition and dissent in the name of stability. Its support for markets and religion varies.

ideologies.name: neo-fascism
ideologies.desc: Neo-fascism is a set of post-1945 movements that draw on fascist ideas, including ultranationalism, authoritarian rule and hostility to liberal democracy. Many deny or play down the crimes of the fascist regimes. Groups differ in method and openness.

ideologies.name: white nationalism
ideologies.desc: White nationalism holds that white people form a race and nation that should have its own states or hold a dominant place in existing ones. It backs racial limits on citizenship and migration. Mainstream science rejects its racial claims, and its movements have a record of racial violence.

ideologies.name: identitarianism
ideologies.desc: The identitarian movement defends what it calls the ethnic and cultural identity of European peoples. It opposes mass migration and multiculturalism and backs the right of peoples to rule themselves. It stresses rooted community and ethnopluralism.

ideologies.name: alt-right
ideologies.desc: The alt-right is a loose online far-right movement of the 2010s that joins white identity politics, hostility to liberalism and multiculturalism, and internet culture. It rejects mainstream conservatism. Members disagree on goals, and many groups hold racial views.

ideologies.name: perennial traditionalism
ideologies.desc: Perennial traditionalism follows Rene Guenon and Julius Evola. It holds that one primordial wisdom lies behind all true religions and that the modern age is a decline. It values hierarchy, ritual and spiritual authority over progress.

ideologies.name: conservative revolution
ideologies.desc: The conservative revolution was a German intellectual movement of the Weimar era, with writers such as Ernst Junger, Oswald Spengler and Carl Schmitt. It rejected liberalism and parliamentary democracy and sought a nationalist, authoritarian renewal.

ideologies.name: bonapartism
ideologies.desc: Bonapartism is rule by a strong leader who claims to embody the will of the people, backed by plebiscites, the army and a centralized state. It joins order, national glory and some social reform. It takes its name from the Bonaparte family of France.

ideologies.name: communitarian conservatism
ideologies.desc: Communitarian conservatism, as in Blue Labour and Red Tory thought, holds that family, locality and faith groups give meaning to life. It holds that markets and the central state can harm them. It backs local ownership, work and mutual aid with traditional morals.

ideologies.name: neo-confucian conservatism
ideologies.desc: Neo-Confucian conservatism draws on Confucian ethics to back social harmony, family duty, respect for rank and rule by educated and virtuous officials. It values order and stable institutions over individual rights and open contest.

ideologies.name: militarism
ideologies.desc: Militarism holds that a strong military should hold a high place in the state. It holds that military values of discipline and obedience should guide public life. It backs high defence spending and the use of force in foreign policy.

ideologies.name: jacobitism
ideologies.desc: Jacobitism backed the restoration of the exiled House of Stuart to the British thrones after 1688. It rested on hereditary right, divine right of kings and, for many, Catholic or Episcopal loyalty. It faded after 1746.

ideologies.name: anarcho-monarchism
ideologies.desc: Anarcho-monarchism is a small current that joins stateless or minimal-state order with a personal monarch or royal house as a private ruler or arbiter. It stresses private law and local rule over a central state.

ideologies.name: aristocratism
ideologies.desc: Aristocratism holds that the best-born or most excellent should rule and that society rests on natural rank and noble duty. It values lineage, honour, culture and service. It doubts equality and mass politics.

ideologies.name: cultural conservatism
ideologies.desc: Cultural conservatism seeks to preserve the heritage, language, customs and norms of a nation or community. It values common culture and is wary of rapid change from migration or new social norms. It need not take a view on economics.

ideologies.name: pronatalist conservatism
ideologies.desc: Pronatalist conservatism treats falling birth rates as a threat to nation, economy and culture, and backs policy and social norms that raise them. It supports marriage, child benefits and family-friendly work and housing.
